final_note: You worked through Static electricity (physics only) — 12 specification statements.

concepts.def: Electric charge that has built up on an object and stays where it is instead of flowing as a current. It is produced when certain insulating materials are rubbed against each other.
When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other, leaving both materials charged.
The movement of negatively charged electrons from one material to another. No charge is created or destroyed; it is only moved.
An object that has gained electrons, so it has more electrons than the positive charge in it can balance.
An object that has lost electrons, so the positive charge left in it is no longer balanced.
The charges produced by rubbing are always equal in size and opposite in sign, because every electron lost by one material is gained by the other.
A material through which charge cannot flow easily, so charge placed on it stays where it is put. Charging by rubbing works with certain insulating materials.
Two objects that carry the same type of charge push each other apart.
Two objects that carry different types of charge pull each other together.
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between charged objects are examples of a non-contact force.
A sudden flow of charge across a gap, seen and heard as a spark, which happens when enough charge has built up on a surface.
When the electric field in a gap becomes strong enough, the air in the gap stops behaving as an insulator and allows charge to flow across, producing a spark.
The region around a charged object in which a second charged object experiences a force.
The electric field is strongest close to the charged object and gets weaker the further away from it you go.

concepts.term: Field pattern for an isolated charged sphere
concepts.def: Straight field lines spreading out radially in all directions from the sphere, evenly spaced around it and closer together near the surface, with arrows pointing away from a positive sphere and towards a negative one.

concepts.term: Force on a second charged object
concepts.def: A charged object placed in an electric field experiences a force, and that force gets stronger as the distance between the two objects decreases.

concepts.term: Field explanation of a non-contact force
concepts.def: Each charged object sits inside the electric field of the other, so each one experiences a force without the two ever touching.
A charged rod hung on a thread so that it can turn freely, used as evidence that a second charged rod brought near it, but not touching, can push it away or pull it round.

mcqs.q: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?
options: Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other one.
Rubbing creates fresh charge on the surface of each material.
Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.
Electrons are rubbed off both materials into the nearby air.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's own account: negatively charged electrons move from one material on to the other, leaving the giver positive and making the receiver negative.

mcqs.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What has happened to the cloth?
options: It has gained some protons from the rod, so it is positively charged.
It has lost electrons to the rod, so it is now positively charged.
It has lost all of its charge, so it now has no charge at all.
It has made new positive charge on its surface while rubbing.
mcqs.explain: The rod became negative by gaining electrons, and those electrons came from the cloth. Losing electrons leaves the cloth with an equal positive charge.

mcqs.q: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material always equal in size to the negative charge on the other?
options: Rubbing always produces equal amounts of the two charges at once.
Both of the materials are rubbed with exactly the same steady force.
Every electron lost by one is an electron gained by the other.
Charge always spreads out evenly between the two materials.
mcqs.explain: The two charges are the two sides of one transfer, so counting electrons on either side must give the same number.

mcqs.q: A student rubs a metal rod held in her bare hand with a dry cloth. The rod shows no sign of being charged. Why not?
options: Metal cannot gain or lose any electrons when it is rubbed.
Rubbing a smooth metal surface is unable to create any charge.
The rod gains and loses equal numbers of electrons as it is rubbed.
Charge on the rod flows away through her hand and body.
mcqs.explain: A metal conducts, so any charge produced does not stay on the rod: it leaks to earth through the student. Charging by rubbing needs an insulating material.

mcqs.q: Two charged objects are brought close together but do not touch. Which statement is correct?
options: Two objects with the same type of charge attract each other.
Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel each other.
The objects only push or pull when their surfaces touch.
Two objects with different charges repel one another.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement: like charges repel, and the force acts without the objects touching.

mcqs.q: Two polythene rods are each rubbed with the same dry cloth. One rod hangs freely on a thread. The second rod is held close to it, without touching. What happens, and why?
options: The hanging rod swings away, because rubbing magnetised them.
The hanging rod swings towards it, because charges attract.
The hanging rod swings away, because both carry a like charge.
The hanging rod stays still until the two rods touch each other.
mcqs.explain: Rubbing both rods in the same way gives both the same type of charge, and like charges repel across the gap between them.

mcqs.q: Which observation is the best evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when they are not in contact?
options: A charged rod picks up small pieces of paper when it touches them.
A rubbed plastic rod picks up small iron filings from a nearby dish.
A rubbed rod feels warmer than it did before it was rubbed.
A hanging charged rod turns away as a like charge is put near.
mcqs.explain: The rod starts to move while a visible gap remains, so the force must be acting across that gap. It is also repulsion, which rules out an uncharged object being attracted.

mcqs.q: A charged polythene rod repels a second charged polythene rod. A student says this shows that rubbing has magnetised the rods. Why is the student wrong?
options: The force is electrostatic; rubbing only moves electrons.
Magnets repel across a gap, so the two effects must be the same.
Magnetism can only act when two poles are brought into contact.
Two magnetised rods would always attract one another instead.
mcqs.explain: Rubbing transfers charge, it does not magnetise. Polythene is not a magnetic material, and the rods behave differently from magnets.

mcqs.q: A student walks across a nylon carpet and then feels a small shock as her hand nears a metal door handle. What has happened?
options: The carpet made new charge, which was stored in the metal handle.
Charge jumps from her hand only once her skin has touched it.
Friction charged her up, and charge then crossed the air as a spark.
The flash is caused by heat from the friction of her shoes.
mcqs.explain: Rubbing between shoes and carpet transfers electrons, charging the student. The charge then crosses the gap to the earthed handle as a spark.

mcqs.q: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps across a gap to a nearby earthed metal pipe. Why does the spark happen?
options: Air can never conduct, so the light must come from the metal pipe.
Charge can only cross a gap at the moment two surfaces touch.
The charge on the object grows heavy enough to fall across.
The field grows strong enough for the air in the gap to conduct.
mcqs.explain: As charge builds up, the electric field across the gap grows. Once it is strong enough the air stops insulating and charge flows across, which is the spark.

mcqs.q: Two acetate rods are each rubbed with a dry cloth and both become positively charged. In terms of electrons, why do the rods then repel each other?
options: Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the like charges repel.
Each rod gained protons from its cloth, so both are now positive.
Rubbing made positive charge on each rod, which pushes them apart.
Each rod lost an equal amount of charge, so the forces balance.
mcqs.explain: Losing electrons leaves each rod positively charged, and two objects carrying the same type of charge push each other apart.

options: A set of paths that a charged object has to follow.
A region in which a charge experiences a force.
Only the lines drawn around a charge on a diagram.
The charge that has built up on a rubbed object's surface.
mcqs.explain: A charged object creates a field around itself, and a second charged object placed anywhere in that region feels a force.

mcqs.q: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change as you move further away from the sphere?
options: It gets stronger, because the field spreads out as it goes out.
It stays the same up to the last line and then stops there.
It stays exactly the same all around the charged sphere.
It gets weaker; the field is strongest close to the charged sphere.
mcqs.explain: The specification states it directly: the field is strongest close to the object and the further away you go, the weaker it is.

mcqs.q: A charged object is moved closer to a second charged object. What happens to the force between them?
options: The force gets stronger as the distance between them decreases.
The force stays the same, as it depends only on the two charges.
The force gets weaker, because the two fields start to cancel.
There is no force at all until the two objects touch.
mcqs.explain: The second object sits in a field that is stronger closer in, so the force on it increases as the gap closes.

mcqs.q: Which description matches the electric field pattern that should be drawn for an isolated charged sphere?
options: Circles drawn all the way round the sphere, all evenly spaced out.
Straight lines spreading out from the sphere in all directions.
Straight lines that always point inwards, towards the sphere itself.
Lines that get closer together further out from the sphere.
mcqs.explain: The pattern is radial: straight lines evenly spaced all around the sphere, closer together near the surface, with arrows away from a positive sphere.

mcqs.q: How does the idea of an electric field help to explain the force between two charged objects that are not touching?
options: Each object sends out lines that pull the other one along them.
The objects interact only if a field line joins one to the other.
Each object sits in the other's field, so each feels a force.
The air between the objects passes the push from one to the other.
mcqs.explain: The field fills the space around each charged object, so neither one has to reach the other: each is already inside a region where it experiences a force.

mcqs.q: A rubbed polythene rod is negatively charged and the cloth that rubbed it positively charged. They are held close but not touching. What happens?
options: They repel each other across the gap.
They attract each other across the gap.
The forces cancel out, so neither moves.
No force acts on either until they touch.
mcqs.explain: Rubbing left the rod and the cloth with opposite types of charge, and two objects carrying different charges pull together without touching.
